sections.heading: Abstract
sections.where: Title page, White Paper v1, May 19, 2025
paragraphs: The paper presents Alpenglow as consensus for a worldwide, high-throughput proof-of-stake chain. Votor, the voting piece, is claimed to finish a block after one voting round when participation covers 80 percent of stake, and after two voting rounds when responsive stake is only 60 percent. The two modes run together. Once the block has already been spread, finalization time is the smaller of one delay among the 80 percent and two delays among the 60 percent, written min(δ80%, 2δ60%).

Rotor, the piece that spreads blocks quickly, relies on erasure coding. Nodes that take part contribute outgoing bandwidth in proportion to stake, so a lone leader link is no longer what caps throughput. The paper claims the nodes’ combined bandwidth is consumed in an asymptotically optimal way. Resilience is labeled “20+20”: harsh network conditions may coincide with an adversary holding 20 percent of stake, and a further 20 percent of stake may sit offline when the assumptions on the network are stronger.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: The paper opens from a disputed remark often linked to Thomas J. Watson, and from a similar remark linked to Howard H. Aiken, and shifts the idea toward a small number of world computers. A world computer, in this telling, accepts transactions as commands and updates an internal bookkeeping state, while offering one shared environment to users everywhere. The machine itself is spread over the world: dozens, hundreds, or thousands of processors, joined by the internet, replace a single processor.

Fault tolerance is the stated gain over even an advanced traditional computer. Many separate components can crash and the shared machine continues, and no authority is in a position to corrupt it for the remaining users. It must also continue if a hostile botnet controls some of those components. The paper treats “blockchain” as the ordinary name for this machine, then introduces Alpenglow as its new protocol.

Rotor is presented as a simpler, tuned descendant of Turbine, the dissemination protocol Solana already uses. Turbine is credited with carrying erasure-coded dispersal into permissionless chains. Because Rotor draws on every node’s available bandwidth, the paper says throughput is asymptotically optimal. Designs that leave the leader’s link as the choke point are said to remain low-throughput.

Votor takes the simple structure of the Simplex research line and recasts it for proof of stake, so leaders rotate without a heavy view-change subprotocol. The common-case claim is one voting round until finality. A more cautious path that uses two voting rounds runs in parallel and is the backup.

sections.heading: Alpenglow Overview
paragraphs: Alpenglow runs on n computers called nodes, and n may be in the thousands or the tens of thousands. That set is known and stays fixed for a period called an epoch. Any node can send a direct message to any other node in the set. The protocol is proof of stake: each node has a known cryptocurrency stake that signals how much the node contributes. If one node has twice the stake of another, it also earns twice the fees and provides twice the outgoing network bandwidth.

Time is cut into slots. Every slot carries a number and a designated leader, and that leader owns a fixed run of consecutive slots (the leader window). A threshold VRF selects who leads which slot. During its turn the leader gathers every new transaction, from users directly or via other nodes, and assembles a block. Slices inside the block let construction be pipelined. Shreds inside each slice provide fault tolerance and spread the bytes evenly.

Dissemination is Rotor, built on erasure coding, so outgoing bandwidth is used in proportion to stake and the leader’s own link is not the bottleneck. The leader hands shreds to relay nodes, and each relay passes its shred on to the other nodes. The moment one block is finished, the following leader begins assembling and spreading the next block. Concurrently, every node comes to hold the block that was just built. Shreds and slices that arrive are kept in the Blokstor.

Nodes then vote on support for the block. Several vote kinds, plus certificates that bundle them, live in a local structure called the Pool. Under Votor, a correctly built block that shows up in time receives a vote. A block that shows up too late draws a skip suggestion, on the grounds that the leader is untrustworthy or the network is unstable. A notarization certificate is formed once a super-majority of all stake has voted for the block, and a notarized block may be finalized at once. When something fails, a fallback path can notarize and finalize, or it can skip.

A later part of the protocol covers how a leader creates blocks and decides where the new block is appended. Repair then lets a node fetch absent shreds, slices, or whole blocks from peers, so it can retrieve an earlier block it missed once that block is an ancestor of a finalized block. The paper says this completes the main consensus discussion.

Correctness comes next. Safety means the outcome stays right even when the network cannot be trusted. Liveness means new blocks keep being decided when the network can be trusted. A further argument looks at many crash failures at once. The paper then points to material that helps understanding even though correctness does not rest on it: a new way to sample Rotor relays, rewards for honest participation, and the path by which transactions are executed.

The same later section then turns to failure handling. It describes how a node reconnects after connectivity drops, and how the system can resynchronize after severe network outages. It adds dynamic slot times to resolve a crisis, and it discusses insufficient bandwidth. The paper closes that roadmap with possible protocol parameters and with measurement results: Alpenglow is simulated on Solana's current node and stake distribution, once for bandwidth and once for latency. The rest of the introduction is reserved for security goals, performance metrics, the model, and the cryptographic tools.

sections.heading: Fault Tolerance
paragraphs: Safety and security are treated as the primary goals for consensus designs. The usual target is withstanding adversaries that hold as much as 33 percent of the stake, the bound also known as "3f + 1". The paper recalls that Pease, Shostak, and Lamport studied that bound in 1980 for systems in which the number of nodes was small, while today's blockchains consist of thousands of nodes. The 33 percent bound still holds for large n, but attacking one or two nodes is a different undertaking from attacking thousands.

Fielding a thousand malicious, or byzantine, nodes would be expensive. The paper puts the likely staking capital in the billions of USD, and notes that punishable misbehavior would forfeit that capital. It expects a real large proof-of-stake deployment to sit well under 33 percent byzantine stake. The failures it treats as realistic are misconfigured machines, software bugs, and losses of network or power, so big outages look like accidents more often than like planned attacks.

That picture is why the paper reopens the familiar “3f + 1” fraction. Alpenglow follows the “5f + 1” fraction introduced by Martin and Alvisi. The paper calls this fraction less forgiving of a classic byzantine attacker, with compensating benefits. A strong adversary forces two voting rounds before finality. With less adversarial stake, or with an adversary that is not misbehaving the whole time, a correct protocol at this fraction can finish in one voting round. The later safety and liveness arguments rest on Assumption 1.

Assumption 1, called fault tolerance, puts byzantine stake strictly under 20 percent, and treats the complementary stake, more than 80 percent, as correct. The protocol is partially synchronous. The paper says this assumption already protects safety when an adversary owns the network outright and can read, hold, and reorder traffic among correct nodes. An outage or a partition pauses progress and lets the protocol resume after communication returns, with no wrong decision in between.

If the network is not under attack, or the adversary does not use a network advantage, the paper says Alpenglow can tolerate a still higher share of nodes that simply crash. Assumption 2, named extra crash tolerance, says byzantine nodes control less than 20 percent of the stake; another cohort totaling up to 20 percent may crash; and the remaining nodes, controlling more than 60 percent of the stake, are correct. The difference between the two assumptions is left to the later crash-resilience discussion.

sections.heading: Performance Metrics
paragraphs: The paper claims the resulting consensus latency is as fast as the setting allows. Once a block has been spread, finalization takes min(δ80%, 2δ60%). Here δθ means how long messages take among a stake-weighted share θ of the nodes; the model section defines it. The protocol gets that bound by running an 80 percent vote and a 60 percent vote at the same time. A geographically tight group holding 60 percent is likely to win on the two-delay path, while nodes farther out may win on the single-delay path. The recorded finalization time is whichever of those finishes first.

Low latency is treated as a main factor in usability, because faster finality gives users results with minimal delay. Throughput, the other main pain point, is measured in transaction bytes per second or in transactions per second. On throughput, the paper says the protocol uses the total available bandwidth asymptotically optimally. After those two metrics, it also wants protocol overhead kept small, including computational requirements and other resource demands.

Simplicity is an explicit goal wherever the design can keep it. The paper calls simplicity hard to measure and still worth having, because arguments about correctness and the job of implementing the protocol both get easier. Later changes and speedups are also easier to make in a protocol that stays simple.

sections.heading: Model and Preliminaries
paragraphs: Objects are written in the form Name(x, y), meaning a deterministic encoding of an object type together with its parameters. To allow changing participants, the protocol rejuvenates itself at regular intervals, and the time between two such changes is an epoch. Epochs are numbered e = 1, 2, 3, and so on. Who participates and with what stake in epoch e+1 is fixed when epoch e-1 ends: registration and unregistration happen two epochs earlier, long enough before epoch e+1 starts, so that everyone agrees on the current nodes and their stake when epoch e+1 begins.

There are n nodes, labeled v1 through vn. They send and relay messages and they check blocks, which is why other writing sometimes calls them validators. Membership changes when the epoch changes and stays fixed inside an epoch. The membership list is public. Every node can address every vi by IP address and port, each node holds a public key, and those keys are known to the whole set. A transaction on the chain publishes and updates that record, so the view of membership is shared. The paper puts Solana’s present size at about 1,500 nodes, and says the protocol can grow further, for example toward about 10,000.

Nodes exchange authenticated messages, and the protocol never uses large ones: every message is less than 1,500 bytes. Communication is UDP with authentication, either QUIC-UDP or UDP with a pairwise message authentication code. The symmetric keys are derived by a key-exchange protocol that uses the public keys. When a node must broadcast the same message to all other n−1 nodes, it loops over the recipients and sends to one node after another. The paper says the total delay is still dominated by the network delay.

On a 1 Gb/s link, pushing n = 1,500 shreds occupies 18 ms. The paper sets that figure well under a typical network delay of about 80 ms. Covering 80 percent of stake means reaching about 150 nodes, which occupies only about 2 ms. Votes are smaller than shreds, so they occupy still less send time. A multicast service from another network, with DoubleZero and SCION named as examples, is also allowed.

Node vi carries a known positive stake amount. The symbol ρi > 0 is vi's fraction of the entire stake, and the fractions sum to 1. Each fractional stake stays fixed during the epoch. Stake signals contribution: if v2 has twice the stake of v1, v2 earns roughly twice the fees and also has twice the outgoing network bandwidth. Every node still needs enough inbound capacity to take in the blocks, plus some floor of outbound capacity to distribute blocks when it is leader.

Every node keeps a local clock of ordinary accuracy, with 50 ppm given as an example drift. The analysis ignores drift, and the paper says an assumed drift can be absorbed into the timeout lengths. No cross-node clock agreement is required, because a node consults only its own clock. Slots partition an epoch. A slot is a natural number attached to a block, and nodes need not agree on when it starts. Local start and end times may differ, although ordinary network conditions pull the slots into rough alignment.

Inside an epoch the slots run s = 1, 2, and so on up to L. The paper says Solana’s present choice L = 432,000 would work, and that a much shorter epoch, for example about 18,000 slots, could help, one reason being faster stake changes. A deterministic leader(s), fixed before the epoch, names the leader of each slot. That leader owns a fixed consecutive run, the leader window. Before the epoch, a threshold verifiable random function produces the public schedule of leaders.

Timeouts keep the protocol from waiting forever for messages. They are based on a global parameter ∆, the maximum network delay between any two correct nodes while the network is synchronous. For simplicity the paper conservatively takes ∆ as a constant, for example ∆ ≈ 400 ms. It can be tuned for a particular leader, estimated from measurements, and adjusted during execution. If the network becomes slow, ∆ might increase; if the network recovers, ∆ can decrease.

Byzantine nodes may deviate in any way, including silence, and they may coordinate. Signing contradictory statements can be a provable offense. A merely late message cannot be punished, because an unusual network delay could explain it. Assumption 1 caps combined byzantine ownership at strictly less than 20 percent of stake. The crash section allows up to another 20 percent of stake to be crashed. Everyone else is correct and follows the rules. From the safety argument through the crash argument, the adversary is treated as fixed for one epoch.

The network is the partially synchronous model with an unknown Global Stabilization Time. Traffic between correct nodes does arrive, and until GST the wait may be arbitrarily long. Safety is unconditional: delays of any size still leave correct nodes emitting one common block order. Liveness holds only in synchronous periods, when delivery is prompt, so correct nodes keep emitting transactions while inter-node messages arrive inside the time bound. After GST, a message m sent at tm is delivered by max(GST, tm) + ∆.

While the network is synchronous, a timeout is seldom what the protocol waits for. Real delay among correct nodes is δ, far below ∆. That δ varies, is unknown, and is not configured into the protocol; latency arguments are its only use. In the common case the paper says an optimistically responsive design such as Alpenglow tracks δ rather than the timeout ceiling ∆. The mark δθ is the time for a stake share θ to exchange messages. Take any set S whose stake sums to at least θ. One interval δθ is enough for every member of S to send to every member of S. When the nodes that hold 60 percent sit near one another, two intervals at 60 percent can beat one interval at 80 percent, because the larger share pulls in more distant stake.

A blockchain here is a growing sequence of finalized transaction blocks, with every node applying those transactions in one shared order. Each block names a parent, beginning from a notional genesis block, and finalized blocks make one parent-child chain. Finalizing a block also finalizes everything above it in that chain. Slot numbers are the natural numbers that order the blocks, and a child’s slot is numerically above its parent’s slot. Each slot ends as either a finalized block from its leader or a skip. Blocks from finalized slots pass upward to execution in slot order. What counts as finalization is defined later.

The safety claim: after any correct node has finalized block b in slot s, every block any correct node finalizes in a slot numbered s or above must be a descendant of b. The paper ties that claim to its safety theorem. The liveness claim: whenever synchrony lasts long enough, correct nodes finalize fresh blocks that correct nodes produced. The paper ties that claim to its liveness theorem.

sections.heading: Cryptographic Techniques
paragraphs: The cryptographic toolkit starts with a collision-resistant hash, SHA256 given as one example, and with digital signatures that outsiders cannot forge. Public keys are common knowledge across the node set. Signatures by different holders can be folded together, with no extra interaction, into one aggregate. The paper needs only the multi-signature case, where every signer covers the same message, and mentions BLS as a way to build that. Short certificates are the reason aggregation is used.

Integer parameters satisfy Γ ≥ γ ≥ 1. A (Γ, γ) erasure code turns a bit string M of length m into Γ pieces d1 through dΓ. Each piece has length m/γ plus an O(log Γ) index. Any γ pieces rebuild M. Rebuild also needs the length m, held constant by padding short payloads. Slice payloads use a Reed-Solomon code with those same parameters, so any γ pieces rebuild the slice. Expansion is the ratio κ = Γ/γ.

A Merkle tree is the commitment to pieces d1 through dΓ. Leaves are the piece hashes inside a full binary tree. A leaf marker is concatenated onto each leaf hash, and every internal node hashes its two children. The root r is the commitment. For index i, the validation path πi is the sibling hashes from the leaf of di up to r. Showing r and πi shows that di occupies position i. Checking recomputes that path and demands the same root. Collision resistance blocks any other string from proving the same position.

The encode function takes a payload M of size m, erasure-codes it into d1 through dΓ, and builds a Merkle tree on the hashes of those pieces. The root r is uniquely associated with M. Encode returns r together with each piece and its path. Decode takes r and a set of γ pairs (di, πi), each of the correct length and each a valid piece at its position for that root. It must also check that r is the root of all Γ pieces of some correctly encoded message, or it fails. A failure guarantees that no set of γ pieces tied to r admits decoding, and that r was constructed maliciously in a provable way.

The pass-or-fail check works by reconstructing a candidate message from the γ pieces, encoding that candidate again into a full vector, and building a new Merkle tree. If the new root equals r, decode returns the candidate. If the roots differ, decode fails. The paper says the check is applied so that every reconstructed piece corresponds to the same root r.

sections.heading: The Alpenglow Protocol
paragraphs: This part of the paper is the detailed account of Alpenglow, after the overview, the fault model, and the cryptographic tools. It specifies the data objects a block is built from how the block is spread, where shreds and votes are kept, how a node votes, how a leader builds the next block, and how missing data is fetched. It then gives the safety and liveness arguments, including the case with extra crash faults.

sections.heading: Shred, Slice, Block
paragraphs: Block bytes are arranged as a double Merkle tree. Every slice contributes a root hash, and those roots become leaves of a second tree whose root is the hash of the whole block. A shred is sized for one UDP datagram. Its fields are slot s, slice index t, shred index i, a one-bit flag zt, a slice root rt, a data piece di with Merkle path πi, and a signature σt. That signature is leader(s) on the object Slice(s, t, zt, rt). The path proves di sits at index i under rt.

Rotor’s input unit is the slice. Decoding needs any γ shreds out of Γ. The slice record holds slot s, index t, the flag zt, root rt, payload Mt, and signature σt. The flag zt marks whether this slice is the last one. Mt is what the shred pieces decode to under rt, and σt is again leader(s) on Slice(s, t, zt, rt). The shred is what crosses the network; the slice is what Rotor is asked to spread.

A block is the sequence of all slices of one slot, and it is the object voting and consensus act on. For slices t = 1 through k, the last flag zk equals 1 and every earlier flag zt equals 0. The block data M is the concatenation of the slice payloads M1 through Mk. The slot of the block is s. Inside M the block records the slot and the hash of its parent. The paper also says each block is limited to a bounded number of bytes and a bounded amount of execution time.

hash(b) is the root of a Merkle tree T built on the slice roots. T is the smallest complete full binary tree whose leaf count m is a power of two and is at least the slice count k. Leaves 1 through k hold r1 through rk, each joined to a marker that identifies a leaf hash. Extra leaves are empty, written bottom. Walking parent links from a block reaches its ancestors, and the walk includes the block itself. A descendant is the opposite direction along those links. Every block counts as its own ancestor and its own descendant.

sections.heading: Rotor
paragraphs: Rotor is Alpenglow’s block dissemination protocol. The leader wants to broadcast a block to every other node with low latency, with bandwidth used in a balanced way, and with resilience to transmission failures. Production and transmission are streaming: the leader does not wait until the whole block exists. A block uses several rounds of Rotor, and each round transmits one slice independently. The leader sends each slice as soon as that slice is ready, which pipelines production and transmission.

On every slice the leader produces Γ Reed-Solomon shreds, hashes them into a Merkle tree, and signs that root. Each coding shred includes its path and the root signature, and it is packed to the capacity of one UDP datagram. Any γ of those shreds rebuild the slice. The extra shreds are the price of that redundancy. After rebuilding, the receiver also regenerates the shreds it never saw, as many as Γ − γ, and uses them as another validity check.

Relays are chosen per slice. The leader gives each shred straight to the node sampled as that shred’s relay. The sampling rule, which the paper says raises resilience, is specified in a later section. The relay then fans the shred out to everyone still missing it, which is everyone but the leader and the relay, ordered from larger stake to smaller stake. A small shortcut sends the next leader its copy before the others, shaving latency for the node that must have the block soonest.

A receiver must check authenticity before reconstructing a slice from γ shreds. The Merkle tree over the shreds of a slice makes that check cheap for each shred on its own: the shred carries its path, and the leader’s signature covers the root. On the first shred of a slice, the node checks the Merkle path and the leader’s signature, then stores the verified root. On every later shred of that slice, the node checks only the Merkle path against the stored root.

A latency figure compares average and median Rotor latency for different expansion ratios, all with γ = 32 data shreds and with the later sampling method. The plotted totals are Γ = 64, 80, 96, and 320, and the latency axis runs up to 120 ms. Red lines mark average and median network latency. With a high expansion rate κ = 10, hence Γ = 320, the paper says the result pretty much reaches the single-δ latency of the latency lemma. All of these simulation results use the Solana stake distribution of epoch 780. Network latency is inferred from public data, and computation and transmission delays are omitted.

Success for slot s means two things: leader(s) is correct, and at least γ relays for that dissemination are correct. Enough correct relays then imply that every correct node obtains the block. A leader that sends no data makes Rotor fail at once. The lemmas that follow assume the leader is correct. The paper says success is likely once coding shreds are over-provisioned by at least 67 percent.

The resilience lemma assumes a correct leader and an expansion κ = Γ/γ strictly greater than 5/3. If γ tends to infinity, a slice is received correctly with probability 1. The sketch samples relays at random according to stake. Each relay's failure probability is less than 40 percent, from the fault-tolerance section. Hence one expects at least 60 percent of Γ relays to be correct, which is strictly greater than 60 percent of 5γ/3, and that quantity equals γ. So strictly more than γ shreds arrive in expectation. A Chernoff bound then gives probability 1 that at least γ shreds arrive correctly at all nodes.

Latency sits between δ and 2δ, depending on optimistic or pessimistic assumptions. If Rotor succeeds, its network latency is at most 2δ. A high expansion factor κ can reduce that latency. In the extreme where n and κ both tend to infinity, network latency can be brought down to δ. The sketch says a correct leader delivers each shred to its relay in time δ, and correct relays deliver onward in another δ, for 2δ in total. With heavy over-provisioning, many correct relays can sit geographically between the leader and a receiver. Under an infinite relay pool plus ordinary assumptions on how stake is spread, at least γ correct relays lie between any leader and any receiver. Relays on the direct path add no extra overhead, so the two legs sum to δ.

Stake is the sampling weight both for who leads and for who relays, so expected transmission tracks stake, just as staking rewards do. Outgoing capacity that scales with stake can be filled, aside from coding overhead. The bandwidth lemma takes a leader whose send rate βℓ is at most the average outgoing rate β̄, and allows any stake-proportional bandwidth assignment. Every correct node then receives block data at expected rate βℓ/κ. The paper calls that optimal once the expansion factor κ = Γ/γ is set aside.

The proof counts how often node vi is chosen as a shred relay: Γρi times in expectation. Each relay receives from the leader at bandwidth βℓ/Γ, because the leader splits its sending across all shred relays. So vi receives from the leader at rate ρi βℓ. It must forward that data to n − 2 other nodes, which in expectation means sending at rate ρi βℓ times (n − 2). Its outgoing bandwidth is βi = n β̄ ρi. Because βℓ is at most β̄, that required rate is strictly less than βi, so every node has enough outgoing bandwidth. The delivered rate cannot exceed βℓ, because only the leader knows the data, and it cannot exceed β̄, because every node must receive the data and the nodes together can send at no more than n β̄. Apart from κ, the paper calls the scheme optimal.

The section closes by limiting what an attack on dissemination can do. Any potential attack on Rotor may affect liveness only. The other parts of Alpenglow still ensure safety under asynchrony, and they rely on Rotor only for data dissemination. A failure to deliver shreds can stall progress, while the voting records that do get observed continue to constrain which blocks may be finalized.

sections.heading: Blokstor
paragraphs: Blokstor is the per-slot archive of slice data that arrived by Rotor, and it keeps the first complete block seen in each slot. An incoming shred is stored only after three checks. No shred with the same slot, slice, and shred index may already be present. The piece and its path must authenticate under the slice root at that index. The signature must be leader(s) on Slice(s, t, zt, rt). Anything that fails a check is dropped.

When Blokstor first holds a complete block b for its slot, it feeds the voting event loop a Block event whose fields are slot(b), hash(b), and hash(parent(b)). Besides the first block of a slot, Blokstor can run repair to fetch some other block and store that block too. If a block is finalized, Blokstor must collect and store only that block in the slot. Otherwise, before the fallback event SafeToNotar for that block's slot and hash is emitted, the block has to be stored in Blokstor as well.

sections.heading: Votes and Certificates
paragraphs: One voting round finalizes a block when the leader collects votes from at least 80 percent of stake; the resulting object is a fast-finalization certificate. Observing votes from 60 percent of stake is what makes a node cast its second-round vote. A second gathering of 60 percent, this time on that second-round vote, finalizes the block too. Stake that finds the block late can instead assemble a skip certificate, and the proposal is then skipped.

Five vote objects are defined, each signed by the voting node. A notarization vote is NotarVote on the slot and hash of a block. A notar-fallback vote is NotarFallbackVote on the same pair. A skip vote is SkipVote on a slot. A skip-fallback vote is SkipFallbackVote on a slot. A finalization vote is FinalVote on a slot. These are the only voting messages the paper lists for a block and a slot.

Certificates aggregate those votes, and Σ is the cumulative stake of the signers in the certificate. A fast-finalization certificate aggregates notarization votes with Σ at least 80 percent. A notarization certificate aggregates notarization votes with Σ at least 60 percent. A notar-fallback certificate aggregates notarization votes or notar-fallback votes with Σ at least 60 percent. A skip certificate aggregates skip votes or skip-fallback votes with Σ at least 60 percent. A finalization certificate aggregates finalization votes with Σ at least 60 percent.

sections.heading: Pool
paragraphs: Every node keeps a Pool that memorizes votes and certificates for every slot. For each slot and each other node, the Pool keeps the first notarization vote or skip vote it receives, up to 3 notar-fallback votes, the first skip-fallback vote, and the first finalization vote. Stake from any one node is therefore counted only once per slot when the later fallback conditions look at notarization and skip votes.

When enough votes have arrived to meet a certificate threshold, the Pool generates that certificate. Whenever a certificate is newly added, whether it was received or built locally, the Pool broadcasts it to all other nodes. For a given block or slot, the Pool stores a single certificate of each type. The thresholds imply a chain: a correct node that generated a fast-finalization certificate also generated the notarization certificate, which likewise means it produced the notar-fallback certificate.

There are two ways to finalize. If the Pool holds a finalization certificate on slot s, the unique notarized block in that slot is finalized, which the paper calls slow-finalized. If the Pool holds a fast-finalization certificate on block b, that block is finalized, which the paper calls fast-finalized. Whenever a block is finalized by either path, all of its ancestors are finalized first.

The Pool emits two events into the voting loop. BlockNotarized carries the slot and hash of a block once the Pool holds a notarization certificate for it. ParentReady(s, hash(b)) is emitted when s opens its leader window, the Pool already holds either a notarization certificate or a notar-fallback certificate covering prior block b, and the Pool holds skip certificates for every slot strictly between b and s.

Fallback events read stake totals the Pool already holds. notar(b) sums the stake behind notarization votes for b. skip(s) sums the stake behind skip votes for slot s. SafeToNotar(s, hash(b)) fires only after this node has voted in s and that vote was not a notarization of b. The numeric test passes if notar(b) is at least 40 percent, or if skip(s) plus notar(b) reaches at least 60 percent while notar(b) is still at least 20 percent. When s opens the leader window, the event is emitted at once. In a later slot, repair fetches b first so the parent is known, and the event waits until the parent’s notar-fallback certificate is also in the Pool.

SafeToSkip(s) is issued only if the node has already voted in slot s and has not voted to skip s. The stake test sums skip(s) with the notarization stake of every block in the slot, then subtracts the largest of those notarization totals, and requires the result to be at least 40 percent. SafeToNotar means it is impossible for a different block to be fast-finalized in the slot, so a notar-fallback vote for this block is safe. SafeToSkip means it is impossible for any block in the slot to be fast-finalized, so a skip-fallback vote for the slot is safe.

sections.heading: Votor
paragraphs: Voting exists to notarize and finalize blocks. Blocks that reach finality assemble into one parent-linked chain and constitute the protocol's output. For every slot the protocol ensures either a skip certificate, or some block that is notarized or notarized in fallback, with all ancestors of that block notarized as well. The thresholds are set so a malicious leader cannot block the certificates liveness needs. If many correct nodes cast notarization votes for the same block, every other correct node casts a notar-fallback vote for it. Otherwise every correct node broadcasts a skip-fallback vote.

Seeing enough notarization votes, cast by others as soon as they got the block, is enough to finalize. The notarization certificate itself uses a lower stake bar, and only after that certificate does the node send a finalization vote. The paper’s summary is one voting round among the stake that holds 80 percent, or two voting rounds among the stake that holds 60 percent. A lifecycle figure of the common case lines up the leader’s send, the relays’ send, notarization votes, and finalization votes, and marks notarization, fast finalization, and slow finalization.

Local clocks drive timeout events. The first ParentReady for a window-opening slot s arms a timer for every slot in that window. Two parameters set the deadlines. ∆block is the block time the protocol specifies. ∆timeout is the longest gap a node should allow between arming those timers and seeing any shred of the next leader’s first block, assuming that block was disseminated correctly. A conservative constant sets ∆timeout to leader-side certificate delay plus Rotor’s dissemination delay, a sum the paper bounds by 3∆.

The schedule for the first ParentReady(s, …) places Timeout(i), for each slot i of the window, at the local clock plus ∆timeout plus (i − s + 1) multiplied by ∆block. Those deadlines are the latest arrival the paper allows when the leader is correct and delivery is synchronous. Finer estimates of ∆, or special cases such as crashes, may shrink the timers. Because ParentReady is raised only on a window’s first slot, the multiplier (i − s + 1) is at least 1, so a timeout is never placed in the past.

Each slot starts with an empty state set, and flags that enter the set stay. ParentReady(hash(b)) means the Pool raised ParentReady for this slot and that hash. Voted means this node has already sent a notarization vote or a skip vote here. VotedNotar(hash(b)) means the notarization vote named that block. BlockNotarized(hash(b)) means the notarization certificate for that block is in the Pool. ItsOver means the finalization vote has been sent and this slot will see no further vote from this node. BadWindow means at least one of skip, skip-fallback, or notar-fallback was sent in this slot. A side array of pending blocks begins at bottom. tryNotar revisits them later, once the parent test might pass.

The event loop is single-threaded. On Block(s, hash, hashparent), the node calls tryNotar. If that call returns true, it runs checkPendingBlocks. If the call returns false and Voted is not yet in the slot state, the block is stored as the pending block for s. On Timeout(s), if Voted is absent, the node calls trySkipWindow(s). On BlockNotarized(s, hash(b)), the node adds BlockNotarized(hash(b)) to the slot state and calls tryFinal. On ParentReady(s, hash(b)), the node adds ParentReady(hash(b)), runs checkPendingBlocks, and calls setTimeouts(s), which starts the timers for every slot in the window.

On SafeToNotar(s, hash(b)), the node first calls trySkipWindow(s). If ItsOver is absent, it broadcasts NotarFallbackVote(s, hash(b)) and adds BadWindow. On SafeToSkip(s), it again calls trySkipWindow(s) first. If ItsOver is absent, it broadcasts SkipFallbackVote(s) and adds BadWindow. The helper windowSlots(s) returns the slot numbers of the leader window that contains s. The helper setTimeouts(s), used when s is the first slot of the window, schedules Timeout(i) for each slot i of that window at the local clock plus ∆timeout plus (i − s + 1) times ∆block.

The helper tryNotar refuses to vote if Voted is already set, and then returns false. Otherwise it tests the parent. When s opens the window, ParentReady for the parent hash must be in this slot's state. If s is a later slot, VotedNotar for the parent hash must be in the previous slot's state. When the test passes, the node broadcasts NotarVote(s, hash), adds Voted and VotedNotar(hash), clears the pending block so it will not cast a second notarization vote, calls tryFinal in case a finalization vote is already justified, and returns true. If the parent test fails, tryNotar returns false.

The helper tryFinal broadcasts FinalVote(s) and adds ItsOver only when three conditions hold together: BlockNotarized for that hash is in the slot state, VotedNotar for that hash is in the slot state, and BadWindow is absent. The helper trySkipWindow walks every slot of the window. For each slot that does not yet contain Voted, it broadcasts SkipVote, adds Voted and BadWindow, and clears the pending block so a notarization vote will not be cast after the skip. The helper checkPendingBlocks walks pending blocks in increasing slot order and calls tryNotar on each one that is not bottom.

sections.heading: Block Creation
paragraphs: The leader v of the window that begins at slot s produces a block for every slot in that window. After ParentReady(s, hash(bp)) is emitted, v knows that a block in slot s with parent bp will be valid: other nodes will receive the same certificates, emit the same event, and vote for the block. In the common case only one such parent event is emitted, so v must build on bp and cannot fork away from the chain. If several parent events are emitted, because the previous leader misbehaved or the network delayed certificates, v may choose any of those parents.

The construction algorithm lets v start optimistically, before any ParentReady event. Usually v sees a block in slot s−1 first, sees a certificate only after another network delay, and only then emits ParentReady. Starting early removes that delay in the common case. If v has been building on bp and the event that arrives names a different parent, v indicates the new parent in the content of some slice t. Slices 1 through t−1 are then ignored for execution. The indicated parent may change only once, and only in a block that occupies the first slot of a window.

Once some ParentReady event has been observed, the leader produces every block of the window without further delays. The first block builds on a parent for which ParentReady was emitted. That block is the parent of the block in the next slot, which is the parent of the block after that and so on. A handover figure with k slices per block shows the new leader emitting the first slice of its first block as soon as it has the last slice of the previous leader. The figure’s upper path is the common case. The lower path is the case in which the new leader switches parents.

The algorithm waits until a block bp in slot s−1 has been received, or until ParentReady for that parent’s hash is in the state of s. It generates a block b in slot s with parent bp and sets the slice index t to 1. While ParentReady is still absent, it disseminates slice t of b through Rotor and increments t. If the ParentReady that eventually appears is not for the original bp, the leader picks any parent that does have a ParentReady record, and generates a replacement block in slot s with that parent, starting at the current slice index t.

After a parent is ready, the leader records the local clock as the start. While the clock is still below that start plus ∆block, it keeps disseminating the next slice of b through Rotor and incrementing t. For each remaining slot s′ = s+1, s+2, and so on it generates a new block whose parent is the block just produced, places that block in slot s′, and disseminates the whole block through Rotor over an interval of ∆block.

sections.heading: Repair
paragraphs: Repair fills in a block whose hash is missing from Blokstor. The trigger is a Pool certificate of signatures on Notar for that slot and hash, or on NotarFallback for the same pair. The bytes that must come back are the block whose hash matches the double-Merkle definition. Four calls support the fetch. sampleNode draws a node with probability proportional to stake. getSliceCount asks that node for the slice count k, the hash rk in leaf position k, and the path πk under the block hash. The caller checks that rk is the last occupied leaf and that hashes to its right on the path are roots of empty subtrees.

getSliceHash asks a node for the slice-root rt at position t and its path under the block hash. getShred asks a node for the shred with slot s, slice t, and shred index i, under the expected slice root rt, in the shred format defined earlier. Any of these functions can fail verification of what the contacted node returns, or find that the node does not have the data, and then return bottom.

The repair algorithm starts with the slice count unknown. It repeatedly calls getSliceCount on a freshly sampled node until k, rk, and πk come back. It then handles slices t = 1 through k concurrently. For each slice, while the slice hash is missing, it calls getSliceHash on a sampled node. For each shred index of that slice, also concurrently, while the shred with indices s, t, and i is missing, it calls getShred on a sampled node and stores the shred if the shred is valid.

sections.heading: Safety
paragraphs: For the proofs, a certificate counts as existing once some correct node has seen it. An ancestor in a given slot counts as existing when parent pointers, followed from a block through the hashes the blocks carry, land on that ancestor. The opening lemma limits a correct node to a single choice per slot between a notarization vote and a skip vote. Both helpers, tryNotar and trySkipWindow, refuse to send either vote once Voted is present, and both insert Voted as soon as they send one. A second vote of either kind in that slot is therefore impossible.

If a block b is fast-finalized, three exclusions follow. No other block in the same slot can be notarized. No other block in the same slot can be notarized in fallback. No skip certificate can exist for the slot. Fast finalization means nodes holding at least 80 percent of the stake cast notarization votes for b. Byzantine stake is less than 20 percent, so correct voters whose stake exceeds 60 percent (call that set V) notarized b. By the one-vote lemma, nodes in V cannot skip the slot or notarize a different block, so notarization stake for any other block is smaller than 40 percent.

Correct nodes cast a notar-fallback vote only when the Pool emits SafeToNotar. That event for a different block requires either at least 40 percent notarizing that other block, or at least 60 percent notarizing it or skipping the slot. Only nodes outside V, holding less than 40 percent, can cast those votes, so no correct node notar-falls-back the other block. A skip-fallback vote is cast only on SafeToSkip, which requires at least 40 percent skipping or notarizing a different block. Again only stake outside V, less than 40 percent, can supply those votes. No correct node skip-falls-back, and no node in V skips or skip-falls-back.

If a correct node cast a finalization vote in a slot, it did not cast a notar-fallback vote or a skip-fallback vote there. Casting the finalization vote adds ItsOver, and the fallback broadcasts are guarded by the absence of ItsOver. In the other order, a notar-fallback or skip-fallback vote adds BadWindow, and tryFinal requires BadWindow to be absent. The two kinds of vote therefore exclude each other in either order.

If correct nodes holding more than 40 percent of the stake notarize the same block b, no other block can be notarized in that slot. A different notarized block would need 60 percent notarization stake, which would include some node from that correct set voting twice, contradicting the one-vote lemma. Thus a slot admits notarization of only a single block: a notarization certificate needs 60 percent, byzantine stake is less than 20 percent, so correct nodes holding more than 40 percent notarized the block, and the previous lemma rules out every other block.

A block finalized by a correct node is also notarized. On the fast path, at least 80 percent notarized it. Byzantine stake is less than 20 percent, so correct nodes holding more than 60 percent broadcast notarization votes, and correct nodes observe a notarization certificate. On the slow path, at least 60 percent cast a finalization vote, including some correct node. A correct node casts that vote only after BlockNotarized is in its state, which means it saw a notarization certificate, and the uniqueness lemma says that certificate is for this block.

Slow finalization has the same three exclusions as fast finalization: no other notarized block, no other notar-fallback block, and no skip certificate in the slot. Slow finalization means at least 60 percent cast finalization votes. Byzantine stake is less than 20 percent, so correct nodes holding more than 40 percent cast those votes. Each of them saw a notarization certificate, and uniqueness forces it to be the same block, for which they had already cast a notarization vote. The one-vote lemma and the mutual-exclusion lemma say they cast nothing else in the slot. Because they hold more than 40 percent, and every certificate needs at least 60 percent, no skip certificate and no certificate on a different block can be produced.

If a notarization certificate or a notar-fallback certificate exists for b, some correct node cast a notarization vote for b. Otherwise, with byzantine stake under 20 percent, every correct node would see less than 20 percent notarizing b. Both branches of SafeToNotar require observing 20 percent notarizing b, so no correct node would emit that event, and no correct node would cast a notar-fallback vote. A certificate still needs at least 60 percent in notarization or notar-fallback votes, which is the contradiction.

If a correct node notarizes b in slot s, then in every earlier slot of the same leader window, including s itself, that node notarized the ancestor of b. The first slot of the window has no earlier slot. In a later slot, tryNotar's parent test requires VotedNotar for the parent hash in the previous slot, and that flag is added only when the notarization vote is cast. Induction covers the whole window. If a correct node casts a notar-fallback vote for a block that is not first in its window, then for the parent either a correct node issued a notar-fallback ballot, or correct nodes holding more than 40 percent cast notarization votes. The SafeToNotar conditions require a notarization or notar-fallback certificate on the parent, hence at least 60 percent of those votes, and byzantine stake under 20 percent forces one of the two correct-node conclusions.

If a block is notarized or notarized in fallback, every earlier slot of its leader window contains an ancestor, and for each such ancestor either correct nodes holding more than 40 percent notarized it or a correct node issued a notar-fallback ballot. Some correct node notarized the block, by the certificate lemma, and that node notarized each ancestor in the window. If the parent already has more than 40 percent correct notarization stake, the ancestor lemma applied to those nodes finishes the argument. Otherwise the parent lemma supplies a correct notar-fallback vote or that same 40 percent threshold, and induction walks back through the window.

Take a finalized block bi and another block bk inside the same leader window, with bk’s slot at least as high as bi’s. Any notarization or notar-fallback certificate on bk, seen by any correct node, forces bk to descend from bi. The fast and slow exclusion results already forbid the two blocks from sharing a slot if their parent chains differ, so bk is strictly later and cannot be the window’s opening slot. Some correct node notarized bk, which plants an ancestor of bk in every preceding slot of the window. The ancestor one slot after bi then has, in bi’s own slot, a parent other than bi. That parent is either notarized, notarized in fallback, or backed by correct notarization stake above 40 percent. Each of those alternatives collides with the exclusion results or with notarization uniqueness.

The cross-window lemma takes a finalized bi and a block bk in a different leader window with a higher slot. Whenever any correct node observes a notarization certificate or a notar-fallback certificate covering bk, then bk descends from bi. Write bj for bk's uppermost ancestor that still sits at or after bi's slot and that is notarized or notarized in fallback. If bj shares bi's window, the previous lemma applies. Otherwise some correct node notarized an ancestor of bj in the first slot of bj's window, which required ParentReady on that ancestor's parent. That parent is itself notarized or notarized in fallback. Placing it before bi would mean a skip certificate on bi's slot. Placing it in bi's slot would notarize a different block there. Placing it after bi contradicts the choice of bj as the highest such ancestor. Each case contradicts the exclusion lemmas.

The safety theorem puts those lemmas together. Whenever one correct node has finalized b at slot s, and any correct node finalizes some b′ at a slot number s or larger, b′ has to sit on b’s descendant chain. Finalizing b′ also notarizes it, and the same-window lemma together with the cross-window lemma supply the descendant relation.

sections.heading: Liveness
paragraphs: If a correct node emits ParentReady for the first slot s of a window, it will emit Timeout for every slot of that window. The ParentReady handler calls setTimeouts, which schedules those timeouts. Setting a timeout for a slot therefore means the node previously emitted ParentReady for the first slot of that slot’s window, naming some block hash. If every correct node sets the timeout for a slot, every correct node casts a notarization vote or a skip vote there. The timeout handler calls trySkipWindow unless Voted is already set, and Voted is added only when one of those two votes is cast.

If no set of correct nodes holding more than 40 percent notarizes the same block in a slot, no correct node adds ItsOver there. ItsOver is added only after BlockNotarized is present, that flag arrives only from a notarization certificate, and the certificate needs 60 percent notarization stake. With byzantine stake under 20 percent, more than 40 percent correct notarization stake would be required. The next lemma says that if every correct node sets the timeout, then either every correct node eventually observes a skip certificate, or correct nodes holding more than 40 percent notarize the same block.

The skip-certificate argument assumes no such 40 percent set exists. Because every correct node set the timeout, every correct node sees skip votes or notarization votes from a set S of correct nodes holding at least 80 percent of the stake, by Assumption 1. After a node v in S has those votes, skip stake plus all notarization stake equals 80 percent plus w, where w is the stake outside S whose skip or notarization vote v has seen. No correct set above 40 percent notarized one block, so the largest notarization total is at most 40 percent plus w. Subtracting that maximum leaves at least 80 percent plus w minus 40 percent minus w, which equals 40 percent. That is the SafeToSkip threshold. If v has not already skipped, it emits SafeToSkip. ItsOver is absent, so v casts a skip-fallback vote. Every correct node therefore skips or skip-falls-back, and every correct node observes a skip certificate.

If correct nodes holding more than 40 percent notarize a block b, every correct node observes a notar-fallback certificate for b. The argument is an induction on how far the slot sits from the first slot of its window. In the first slot, a correct node that has not notarized b and has not notar-fallen-back will still see more than 40 percent notarization stake and will emit SafeToNotar. It cannot have added ItsOver, because a finalization vote would require it to have notarized some notarized block, and uniqueness says that block would have to be b. The SafeToNotar handler then sees ItsOver absent and casts the notar-fallback vote. So every correct node votes notarization or notar-fallback, and the certificate is observed.

For a later slot, the same supposition is used. A correct node that has not yet voted notarization or notar-fallback for b still sees more than 40 percent and by the fallback rule, retrieves b and identifies its parent. The correct nodes that notarized b also notarized that parent in the previous slot. The induction hypothesis gives a notar-fallback certificate on the parent, so SafeToNotar fires, ItsOver is still absent, and the node casts the notar-fallback vote. Again every correct node observes the notar-fallback certificate.

If every correct node sets the timeouts for a window, then for every slot in the window every correct node observes either a notar-fallback certificate for some block in that slot or a skip certificate for the slot. A slot with no skip certificate must by the previous alternative, have more than 40 percent correct notarization stake on one block, and that block then has a notar-fallback certificate. From there, every correct node emits ParentReady for the first slot of the next window. If the whole window is skipped, the parent certificate that opened this window, together with the new skip certificates, satisfies ParentReady for the next window. If some highest slot lacks a skip certificate, its notar-fallback certificate plus skip certificates on every later slot up to the next window do the same.

Every correct node therefore sets the timeouts for every slot, by induction from the timeout-scheduling lemma and the next-window lemma. After GST, once the earliest correct node arms the timeout on the window's opening slot s at time t, every correct node emits some ParentReady for s and sets the window's timeouts by time t + Δ. That first node had already observed the notar-fallback certificate and the intervening skip certificates by time t, and it broadcast them, so they arrive at every correct node within one Δ.

The liveness theorem names a correct leader vℓ of a window that begins at slot s. No correct node set the window’s timeouts before GST, and Rotor is successful for every slot of the window. Then every block vℓ produces in the window is finalized by every correct node. The argument has four steps. First it bounds when correct nodes receive the blocks. Then it supposes some correct node v skips, and shows v skips every slot from the first skipped slot through the end of the window. Then it classifies the cause of v’s first skip. Finally it shows the timeout that would cause that skip arrives only after v has already notarized the slot.

Write t for the moment the earliest correct node arms the timeout on s. Because that moment is at or after GST, the leader holds ParentReady for some parent by t + ∆, and the block-construction steps have entered the timed loop by that same instant. Transmission of the block in slot k ends by t + ∆ plus (k − s + 1) times ∆block. Successful Rotor then puts that block in every correct node’s hands by t + 3∆ plus the same multiple of ∆block.

Suppose some correct node v fails to notarize some block of the window, and let k be the earliest such slot. The leader is correct, so the only valid block in slot k is the leader’s block, and v cannot notarize a different one. The timeout lemma makes v cast a skip vote in slot k. The parent test for later slots then prevents v from notarizing any later slot of the window, so v skips every slot from k onward. Skip votes are produced by trySkipWindow, which runs only from SafeToNotar, SafeToSkip, or Timeout on some slot j of the window. Let j be the slot whose handling produced v’s first skip in the window.

SafeToNotar on a slot before k cannot be emitted by a correct node, because every correct node notarized that earlier block. For a slot j at or after k, SafeToNotar requires that v already skipped j, so it cannot be the cause of the first skip. SafeToSkip has the same shape: it is not emitted by a correct node before k, and at or after k it requires a skip that v has already cast. The remaining cause is Timeout(j). That event does nothing if v has already notarized j, and v will not notarize j after the timeout has fired. Since v notarized every slot before k, the index j is at least k. Timeouts in one window are scheduled later for later slots, so the earliest moment of v’s first skip is the moment Timeout(k) fires.

That timeout fires at or after t plus ∆timeout plus (k − s + 1) times ∆block, and the writeup lower-bounds that instant by t plus 3∆ plus the same multiple of ∆block. By the reception bound, v has already received every block from s through k. It has also emitted ParentReady for the parent of the first block. The parent test in tryNotar therefore succeeds for the first slot, and checkPendingBlocks, which runs on both Block and ParentReady, notarizes every block from s through k regardless of arrival order, before Timeout(k) fires. That contradicts the choice of v. Every correct node therefore notarizes every block of the window, every correct node observes the fast-finalization certificate for each of them, and every correct node finalizes them.

sections.heading: Higher Crash Resilience
paragraphs: This section sketches correctness when the network is less adversarial and crash faults are more numerous. In harsh network conditions an adversary with over 20 percent of the stake can attack Alpenglow, and the paper says such an attack needs careful orchestration. Accidental errors, crashes, and DoS campaigns that look like crashes are described as the failures that have historically caused more trouble for blockchains. The rest of the section uses Assumption 2 in place of Assumption 1, and adds Assumption 3 to capture the attacker's weaker control of the network.

Assumption 3 is called Rotor non-equivocation. It says a full block delivered by Rotor to one correct node is the only full block Rotor delivers to any other correct node in that slot. Crashes are identified with delay that never ends. Safety was already argued for delays of unbounded length, and the model permits those delays, so Assumption 2 does not reopen safety. What changes is liveness, in the steps that needed every correct node to gather enough votes for SafeToNotar or SafeToSkip.

With Assumption 3, two correct nodes cannot reconstruct different blocks in the same slot, so after they see the votes of the other correct nodes, every correct node emits either SafeToNotar or SafeToSkip. If correct nodes holding at least 20 percent of the stake notarized a block, then skip stake plus notarization stake is at least 60 percent and notarization stake is at least 20 percent, which is the second SafeToNotar branch. Otherwise skip stake plus all notarization stake, minus the largest notarization total, is at least the skip stake, and that skip stake is at least 40 percent, which is SafeToSkip.

The corollary keeps the liveness theorem, with Assumptions 2 and 3 standing in for Assumption 1. A leader that is correct, or merely crashed, never breaks the non-equivocation assumption, since it emits at most one block in a slot. Pure crash faults below 40 percent of stake are therefore always inside the tolerated set. An adversary that does feed different blocks to different receivers, while many other nodes are crashed, can leave correct nodes short of the votes SafeToNotar and SafeToSkip require. In that case the protocol can stall.

A malicious leader might try to distribute two blocks so that one cohort of correct nodes rebuilds and backs the first while a disjoint cohort rebuilds and backs the second. If a correct node receives two shreds that do not belong to the same block, meaning different Merkle roots for the same slice index, before it can reconstruct, it will not vote for the block. Whether two different blocks can be delivered to two different correct sets therefore depends on network topology and on how Rotor relays are sampled.

The example uses two clusters, A and B, whose internal latency is negligible compared with the latency between them. Each cluster holds 31 percent of the stake. The adversary controls 18 percent, and 20 percent of the stake is crashed. Relays in A receive shreds of one block from the malicious leader, and relays in B receive shreds of a different block. Adversary relays forward the first block’s shreds to A and the second block’s shreds to B. Because of the delay between the clusters, A reconstructs its block before seeing any shred of the other, and B does the same. Assumption 3 fails in this arrangement. If nodes are spread uniformly, the paper says it is harder to arrange for a large group to collect enough shreds of one slice before seeing any shred of the corresponding slice of the other block.

sections.heading: Beyond Consensus
paragraphs: This section turns to issues that sit outside the core consensus argument and still matter for understanding Alpenglow. It starts with three topics close to consensus: how Rotor relays are sampled, how participation is rewarded, and how transactions are executed. It then covers advanced failure handling. It finishes with simulation measurements of bandwidth and of latency.

sections.heading: Smart Sampling
paragraphs: To improve Rotor's resilience in practice, the paper uses a committee sampling scheme inspired by FA1 and intended to improve on FA1-IID by reducing sampling variance further. A partitioning of relative stakes, each strictly between 0 and 1, into k bins is a mapping that assigns every node's stake fully across the bins and fills every bin exactly to 1/k. Any procedure that for any k and any such stakes, yields a legitimate partitioning is termed a partitioning algorithm.

The scheme is called partition sampling, or PS-P, and it is instantiated with a particular partitioning algorithm. One draw of Γ samples works in three steps. First, each node whose relative stake exceeds 1/Γ fills floor(ρi Γ) bins by itself. The leftover stake is the original stake minus that integer count divided by Γ, which is less than 1/Γ. Every other node keeps its original stake as the remainder. Those remainders, each under 1/Γ, are what the unfilled bins receive.

Second, whatever partitioning algorithm was chosen splits the leftover stakes across the bins still empty. How many bins remain is Γ minus the sum of floor(ρi Γ) over all nodes. Third, each bin contributes exactly one sample, drawn with probability proportional to stake inside that bin. One easy partitioner shuffles the nodes and slices the stake line at every 1/k. The paper says even that easy partitioner, inside PS-P, beats the sampling results already in the literature, and that the question is still open for further work.

The comparison is with independent stake-weighted sampling and with FA1-IID. The adversary A may spread a total stake ρA over many nodes. The text assumes ρA is below γ/Γ, equates that ratio with 1/κ, and writes the further relation that γ is below ρA times Γ. For any stake distribution in which every ρi is below 1/Γ, and for any partitioning algorithm, the chance that PS-P samples the adversary at least γ times is at most the chance under IID stake-weighted sampling.

The proof treats the adversary’s sample count, after the per-bin draw, as a Poisson binomial: Γ independent Bernoulli trials whose success probabilities are the adversary’s stake share in each bin. If the adversary is packed equally into all Γ bins, the count is binomial with success probability ρA, the same distribution as IID stake-weighted sampling. That binomial case maximizes the variance among Poisson binomials, and therefore maximizes the probability of at least γ adversarial samples, with the paper writing that threshold as γ below Γ. For an arbitrary stake distribution, the chance of at least γ adversarial samples under PS-P is at most the chance under FA1-IID, because the first step makes the scheme equivalent to FA1 using this scheme as its fallback, and the equal-stake lemma then applies.

The paper then compares the scheme with regular stake-weighted IID sampling and with FA1-IID under today's Solana stake weights. A figure plots the probability that Rotor is unsuccessful under crash failures. PS-P uses fully randomized partitioning. The other curves are FA1-IID, stake-weighted sampling, and Turbine. The figure assumes 64 slices per block, and Rotor succeeds for the block only if it succeeds for every slice. One panel is crashes with γ = 32 and Γ = 64, against crashed stake of 40 percent, 30 percent, and 20 percent. The other panel is 40 percent crashes at κ = 2, against total shred counts Γ of 64, 128, and 256. The probability axis is marked on a logarithmic scale at 1, 10 to the minus 4, 10 to the minus 8, and 10 to the minus 12. The text does not tabulate the height of each curve.

sections.heading: Rewards
paragraphs: All Alpenglow participation should be rewarded, and the rewards should pay for behavior that keeps the protocol safe and efficient. Rewards are paid directly on the blockchain. Nodes report the participation of other nodes, and that reporting is what triggers payment. The schemes must not become a gamble. Performance and truth should be the most profitable choices. The paper wants to reward participation in Rotor, in Votor, and in Repair.

The leader needs no Rotor reward, because it is already motivated to disseminate its own block. Relays do the heavy bandwidth work and should be rewarded for pushing their shreds out to the rest of the network. For Votor, votes are rewarded. Every node should vote for a block or against it, using a notarization vote or a skip vote. The one-vote lemma says a node is not allowed to cast both. The reward for either vote is the same, so a node is paid to answer truthfully rather than to bet on what others will do.

Repair has a requesting side and a providing side. The paper unifies the accounting because Rotor, Votor, and Repair are all just sending and receiving data. Across epoch e, every node tallies outbound messages toward each peer and inbound messages from each peer. The count may be weighted messages, or even bytes. Each node therefore accumulates two vectors of n integers. In the opening half of epoch e+1, the nodes report both vectors, and the rewards are paid from those reports.

Inventing extra bandwidth is described as hard, because the protocol already knows how many shreds a relay was assigned and will not pay a larger fantasy count. Stake also balances the traffic. Suppose sender vs reports x repair shreds toward receiver vr. That report is implausible when most other nodes vt report having sent vr far less, well under x multiplied by ρt/ρs. A payout function turns the full set of reported vectors into a reward per node. Smaller bonuses sit on facts the chain can see directly. The example given is a bonus for whichever certificate appears first on a block.

sections.heading: Voting vs. Execution
paragraphs: Execution of a block’s transactions was left out of the consensus section. The paper says the model Solana uses today is the synchronous one sketched here. The leader runs the block, and only then transmits it. Every other node runs the block, and only then votes. Pipelined slices let the next slice travel while the previous slice is still running. The last slice still sits on the critical path: its execution finishes before the notarization vote for that block goes out.

The alternative is asynchronous execution, in which nodes vote on a block before executing it. Compute Units then have to reflect actual execution cost. Bounds on Compute Units for each transaction and for the whole block are what keep execution timely. If the Compute Unit accounting is unrealistically optimistic, the approach fails, because execution delay can grow without a bound.

Distributed execution is described as a related research direction. Validators use several machines, placed together so latency stays small, to execute transactions. Compared with execution on one machine, the aim is higher transaction throughput, and the ability to absorb traffic surges without permanently over-provisioning, which the paper calls elasticity. Pilotfish and Stingray are named as examples of that line of work.

sections.heading: Asynchrony in Practice
paragraphs: The model assumed that delayed messages are eventually delivered. The paper notes that this is standard in distributed computing, while in reality, and in the original partial-synchrony formulation with GST, messages can be lost. Alpenglow already allows arbitrarily long delays, so dropping messages does not by itself break safety. This section adds two practical mechanisms that restore liveness when the protocol is making no progress.

A node may go offline and miss every message from that interval. When a node that is rebooting or joining late sees that block b reached finality in slot s, it does not need votes or certificates from earlier slots. The safety theorem says any later block that might be finalized, in a slot at or after s, is a descendant of b. If any correct node emits ParentReady for a later slot and a block, that block is a descendant of b as well.

To come back, a node must see one of two bundles for some slot s and block b. The first bundle is a fast-finalization certificate on b. The second is a finalization certificate on s paired with a notarization certificate on b in that same slot. Repair then pulls in b. With b stored, the parent hash inside it identifies the previous block, which is fetched the same way, and the walk continues. An implementation may download missing blocks across slots at the same time, and only afterward check and repair b’s ancestors.

Progress after GST still depends on messages eventually showing up. A finalization already seen in slot s makes older votes and certificates unnecessary for liveness. Stalls are visible as a run of time in which no higher slot becomes finalized. The parameter given is a standstill of about 10 seconds with the highest finalized slot unchanged. Correct nodes then retransmit. They send out a certificate for the highest finalized slot they know, using whichever bundle they hold: fast-finalization on the block, or finalization of the slot plus notarization of the block. For every slot above that one, they also resend certificates they have seen and votes they cast themselves.

sections.heading: Dynamic Timeouts
paragraphs: Alpenglow's definition uses the partially synchronous model, and the paper says epochs, strictly speaking, deviate from partial synchrony. Epoch changes need at least one finalized block in each epoch. A block finalized in epoch e confirms that epoch e-1 ended in an agreed state. That agreement is what sets up epoch e+1, so that the nodes and their stake are agreed at the start of epoch e+1.

The remedy is to lengthen timeouts when the situation looks dire. If a node has no finalized block across a standstill interval of about 10 seconds of consecutive leader windows, it begins extending its timeouts by about 5 percent in every leader window. Nodes do not need consensus on the moment they start extending; approximate agreement is enough. As soon as finalized blocks appear again, nodes return immediately to the standard timeouts of the voting section. Returning also needs no time consensus, because some nodes may keep longer timeouts without threatening correctness.

Raising timeouts by about 5 percent in every leader window is exponential growth. The paper says that growth makes an epoch last long enough to outlast a network or power disaster. Even though epochs depart from partial synchrony, the paper says it can practically be guaranteed that each epoch contains a finalized slot.

sections.heading: Stake ≠ Bandwidth
paragraphs: The model assumed that each node provides outgoing bandwidth proportional to its stake. That assumption lets Rotor sample relays by stake and is described as the choice with maximum security. The paper says stake equal to bandwidth may not hold in practice, because a node might be unable to deliver the bandwidth its stake promises.

Measurement is the same activity the rewards section already uses. Once an epoch ends, each node publishes, for every other node, how many of that node’s shreds it observed across the rest of the set. The published counts ought to line up, roughly, with the relay assignments those nodes actually received. A gap up to about 5 percent is tolerated. A node that misses by more than that is selected less often afterward.

The performance ratio ϑ divides shreds delivered by shreds commissioned. When ϑ drops below 1 − ε, with ε about 5 percent, the following epoch multiplies that node’s relay-selection probability by ϑ. The shortfall is measured in epoch e−1, reported during the first half of epoch e, and enforced in epoch e+1. The expected steady state is ϑ = 1, called the full stake rate. A node below 1 that still stays inside the 5 percent band, that is within 1 − ε of expected delivery, has its ϑ raised by ε, about 5 percent, on each subsequent epoch, stopping when ϑ returns to 1.

sections.heading: Protocol Parameters
paragraphs: A table gathers parameter choices for the paper’s preliminary simulations, and the text says those choices still need testing before they are settled. Other parameters are implicit and differ by epoch. Node count is the chief example. Earlier sections speak of about 1,500 nodes, while the paper says the live count when it was written sits nearer 1,300.

The simulation table sets 4 blocks per leader window. Each slice uses γ = 32 data shreds and Γ = 64 coding shreds. The timeout increase ε is 5 percent. The standstill trigger is 10 seconds. The block time ∆block is 400 ms. The epoch length L is 18,000 slots.

sections.heading: Bandwidth
paragraphs: This section measures how much bandwidth Alpenglow’s voting traffic uses. A size table is given for a network of 1,500 nodes, with columns for a BLS signature, a slot number, a block hash, a node bitmap, a MAC, headers, and the total. A notarization vote is 96 + 8 + 32 + 32 + 28 = 196 bytes, with no bitmap. A notarization certificate is 96 + 8 + 32 + 188 + 32 + 28 = 384 bytes. A fast-finalization certificate has the same layout and is also 384 bytes. A finalization vote is 96 + 8 + 32 + 28 = 164 bytes, with no block hash and no bitmap. A finalization certificate is 96 + 8 + 188 + 32 + 28 = 352 bytes, with no block hash. A skip vote is 164 bytes, matching the finalization vote. A skip certificate is 352 bytes, matching the finalization certificate.

As a bandwidth optimization, only one finalization certificate is broadcast, whichever is observed first. In the common case every node broadcasts, for every slot, a notarization vote, a finalization vote, a notarization certificate, and one finalization certificate. Counting the larger finalization certificate, the fast-finalization certificate, a node with n = 1,500 transmits (196 + 384 + 384 + 164) times 1,500 bytes in every 400 ms slot. The paper states that this is 32.27 Mbit/s.

A histogram shows outgoing bandwidth for a consistent goodput of 500 Mbps, the operating point at which the leader must send at 1 Gbps when κ = 2. The curves separate average Rotor traffic from voting traffic. Validators are ordered from small to large, with the axis running through 1,200. The bandwidth axis is logarithmic. The caption gives the 500 Mbps goodput and the 1 Gbps leader rate; the text does not list a bandwidth for each validator.

sections.heading: Latency
paragraphs: Latency numbers come from a simulation the paper runs against a setting it calls realistic. Stake weights are Solana’s as of epoch 780, the distribution at the time of writing, and inter-node delays come from measured wide-area latencies. Execution of blocks is among the delays left out. Changing the stake weights would move the curves. Each run samples Rotor relays at random, weighted by stake.

One histogram fixes the leader in Zurich, the authors’ location at the time of writing. Each bar averages 100,000 simulated executions. The horizontal axis is the fraction of stake that has reached a stage, and the vertical axis runs to 300 ms. Green bars are network latency. With Solana’s node distribution, about 65 percent of the stake is within 50 ms of Zurich, and the long tail is more than 200 ms from Zurich. Network latency is a lower bound: a node 100 ms from Zurich needs at least 100 ms before any protocol can finalize a block there. Yellow bars are Rotor delay, the time until a node has γ shreds and can reconstruct a slice. Red bars mark receipt of notarization votes from at least 60 percent of the stake.

Blue bars are the time until finality. Three events compete, and the earliest wins. The node may assemble a fast-finalization certificate from notarization votes covering 80 percent of stake. It may assemble a finalization certificate from finalization votes covering 60 percent of stake. Or it may be handed either certificate by a third party. With the leader fixed in Zurich and relays drawn at random, finality reaches the slowest node in under 270 ms. The median node finishes nearly as soon as the quickest nodes, at roughly 115 ms.

A second histogram is the same measurement with the leader chosen at random according to stake. The paper says Zurich is more central than the average leader, while it is not the center of the Solana stake map, so the numbers sit a bit higher. The median finalization time in that plot is roughly 150 ms. The same four stages are shown: network latency, Rotor, notarization, and finalization.
